questions.stem: An immobile hospitalized client is at high risk for pressure injury and is lying on a pressure-redistributing support surface. Which repositioning plan is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Individualize the turning frequency based on the support surface, skin response, mobility, perfusion, tolerance, and other risk factors, while continuing regular repositioning.","B":"Use a fixed two-hour schedule for every at-risk client because support surface, tissue tolerance, sleep, perfusion, body size, and individual risk do not alter repositioning needs.","C":"Stop routine repositioning once a pressure-redistributing mattress is in place because the support surface removes clinically meaningful pressure-injury risk.","D":"Reposition only after nonblanchable erythema appears because turning before visible skin injury has not been shown to contribute to pressure-injury prevention."}}
questions.rationale: Current pressure-injury prevention guidance supports regular repositioning but does not require one universal interval for every patient. Frequency should be individualized according to the support surface, tissue tolerance, mobility, perfusion, clinical condition, and patient preferences. A support surface does not eliminate the need to reposition.
questions.source_name: National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel — Pressure Injury Prevention / International Guideline
questions.source_detail: NPIAP guidance supports individualized repositioning frequency based on support surface, skin/tissue tolerance, mobility and other patient-specific risk factors.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client has dry oral mucosa, increasing orthostatic dizziness, reduced urine output, and delayed skin recoil over the forearm. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The delayed skin recoil alone confirms severe dehydration and makes the other findings unnecessary for determining the client's fluid status.","B":"The combined findings raise concern for volume depletion, but skin turgor is less reliable with aging and should be interpreted with the broader assessment.","C":"The client's age makes dehydration unlikely because older adults maintain stronger thirst responses and renal concentrating ability than younger adults.","D":"The findings indicate fluid overload because reduced skin elasticity in older adults is a specific sign of increased intravascular and interstitial fluid volume."}}
questions.rationale: Older adults are especially vulnerable to dehydration, but skin turgor becomes less specific as skin elasticity changes with age. The nurse should integrate symptoms, orthostatic findings, mucous membranes, urine output, intake/output, laboratory data, and the clinical context rather than diagnose dehydration from skin recoil alone.
questions.source_name: Clinical Assessment of Hydration in Older Adults — Evidence-Based Bedside Evaluation
questions.source_detail: Skin turgor has limited diagnostic value for hypovolemia in adults and is less reliable with aging; hydration assessment should integrate multiple clinical findings.

questions.stem: A client has right-leg weakness after hip surgery and is beginning cane training. Which technique provides the best mechanical support during level ambulation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Hold the cane in the right hand and advance it after the stronger left leg so the cane remains on the same side as the weaker extremity during each step of gait.","B":"Alternate the cane between hands every few steps so both upper extremities share the load equally and the client avoids developing a side preference.","C":"Hold the cane in the left hand and advance the cane with the weaker right leg, allowing the device to widen the base of support and unload the affected side.","D":"Place the cane directly in front of both feet and advance both legs together toward it so the device functions as a single central point of balance."}}
questions.rationale: A cane is generally held contralateral to the weaker or painful lower extremity. Advancing the cane with the affected leg helps widen the base of support and reduces load through the involved side. Device choice and gait pattern should still follow the client's postoperative precautions and rehabilitation plan.
questions.source_name: NCBI Bookshelf — Assistive Devices and Gait Training
questions.source_detail: Standard cane gait uses the cane on the stronger/opposite side and advances it with the weaker affected leg unless a patient-specific rehabilitation plan directs otherwise.

questions.stem: A client receiving intermittent gastric tube feedings had nausea and abdominal distention during the previous feeding. Which assessment approach is most appropriate before the next feeding?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use the pump's programmed rate as the sole indicator of tolerance because subjective symptoms, abdominal findings, and stool or flatus patterns do not reliably affect feeding decisions.","B":"Automatically stop all enteral nutrition whenever any measurable gastric residual is obtained, even when the client has no other evidence of feeding intolerance.","C":"Rely only on the presence of bowel sounds because bowel sounds are the most accurate single measure of aspiration risk and gastric emptying in enterally fed clients.","D":"Assess the client's symptoms and abdominal findings and follow the facility's evidence-based protocol; do not rely on a single gastric residual value as the sole tolerance measure."}}
questions.rationale: ASPEN recommends evaluating enteral-feeding tolerance using multiple clinical parameters such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal distention, pain, stool/flatus patterns, physical findings, and the overall clinical course. Gastric residual volume should not be used as a stand-alone determinant of tolerance, and routine GRV monitoring may not be necessary in some settings.
questions.source_name: ASPEN — Safe Practices for Enteral Nutrition Therapy
questions.source_detail: ASPEN recommends a multidimensional assessment of enteral-feeding tolerance and cautions against relying solely on gastric residual volume.

questions.stem: An adult client wants a realistic weekly physical-activity goal for general health. Which plan best matches current U.S. public-health guidance?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity each week and include muscle-strengthening activity on at least 2 days during the week.","B":"Limit activity to one short session each week because additional moderate aerobic activity provides no measurable health benefit in otherwise healthy adults.","C":"Complete at least 10 hours of vigorous exercise every week before adding any muscle-strengthening activity, regardless of baseline fitness or medical history.","D":"Avoid structured physical activity unless weight loss is the primary goal because aerobic and resistance exercise are not recommended for general health maintenance."}}
questions.rationale: CDC guidance recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, or an equivalent amount of vigorous/mixed activity, plus muscle-strengthening activities on at least 2 days each week. Some activity is better than none, and goals can be adapted to the person's condition and abilities.
questions.source_detail: Current CDC guidance: adults need at least 150 minutes/week moderate-intensity aerobic activity plus muscle strengthening on 2 or more days.
